content_html:
This loan calculator works out the regular payment on any fixed-rate amortized loan, such as a personal loan, car loan, student loan or small mortgage. Enter how much you are borrowing, the interest rate and the term, and it shows the payment, the total interest and a full amortization schedule. You can also change how often you pay, test a different compounding basis and see what an extra payment each period would save.

How to use this calculator

  1. Loan amount: the amount you borrow, after any down payment.
  2. Interest rate: the annual rate in your loan offer. For most US consumer loans this is the APR or the note rate, which compounds monthly.
  3. Loan term: the length of the loan in years, plus any extra months (for example 3 years and 6 months).
  4. Payment frequency: monthly is standard. Choose every two weeks, weekly or another schedule if your lender offers it.
  5. More options: change the compounding basis if your agreement states one, or add an extra amount to every payment to see how much sooner you would finish.

How the payment is calculated

An amortized loan has the same payment every period. Early payments are mostly interest because the balance is high; as the balance falls, more of each payment goes to principal. The payment is:

Payment = L × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)−n)

where L is the loan amount, i is the interest rate per payment period and n is the number of payments. With monthly payments and monthly compounding, i is simply the annual rate divided by 12. When the payment and compounding schedules differ, the calculator first converts the annual rate to the equivalent rate per payment, (1 + r/m)m/p − 1, where m is compounding periods and p is payments per year. At a 0% rate the payment is just the loan amount divided by the number of payments.

Worked example

Borrow $20,000 at 8% for 5 years with monthly payments:

  • Monthly rate: 8% ÷ 12 = 0.6667%, over 60 payments.
  • Monthly payment: $405.53.
  • Total of all payments: about $24,331.67, so total interest is $4,331.67, roughly 21.7% of the amount borrowed.
  • Adding $50 to every payment pays the loan off in 53 payments instead of 60 and cuts interest to about $3,741.44, a saving of around $590.

Switching the same loan to payments every two weeks gives 130 payments of $186.83 and slightly less interest ($4,288.15), because the balance is reduced a little more often.

Practical tips

  • Compare loans by APR rather than the interest rate alone, because the APR includes most upfront fees.
  • A lower payment from a longer term can be useful for cash flow, but check the total interest before you commit.
  • Before making extra payments, confirm that your lender applies them to principal and does not charge a prepayment penalty.
  • The schedule assumes every payment is made on time and the rate never changes. Variable-rate loans will differ.

faq.question: What is the difference between an amortized loan and an interest-only loan?
faq.answer: With an amortized loan every payment covers that period's interest plus some principal, so the balance reaches zero at the end of the term. With an interest-only loan the payments cover interest alone for a set period and the principal is still owed afterward.

faq.question: Should I enter the APR or the interest rate?
faq.answer: Enter the note rate (the interest rate) to get the exact payment your lender will charge. The APR also folds in upfront fees, so it is better for comparing offers than for calculating the payment. If the two are close, either gives a useful estimate.

faq.question: Do payments every two weeks really save money?
faq.answer: Yes, a little. Paying every two weeks means 26 half-sized payments a year, the equivalent of 13 monthly payments, so the balance falls faster and less interest builds up. Check that your lender credits each payment when it arrives rather than holding it until the monthly due date.

faq.question: Why is so much of my early payment interest?
faq.answer: Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which is largest at the start. As you pay down principal the interest portion shrinks and the principal portion grows, even though the payment stays the same.

faq.question: Can this calculator handle a loan with a balloon payment?
faq.answer: Not directly. It assumes the loan is fully paid off by the last regular payment. For a balloon loan, the payment is usually calculated over a longer schedule, and the remaining balance at the balloon date is shown in the amortization table for that payment number.
